Identification
Typing a username at a login prompt is an example of which step?
Identification
Authentication
Authorisation
Accounting
Identification claims an identity; authentication proves it.
m
Authentication
Which step proves that a user is who they claim to be?
Authentication
Identification
Authorisation
Federation
Authentication verifies the claim using something the user knows, has or is.
d
Authorisation
A logged-in employee opens a payroll report they should not see. Which step failed?
Authorisation
Identification
Authentication
Encryption
The user was identified and authenticated; the system wrongly permitted the action.
m
Password storage
How should passwords be stored in a database?
As salted hashes from a slow password-hashing algorithm
In plain text so that support staff can read them
Encrypted with one key stored next to the database
As unsalted MD5 hashes for fast comparison
Password-specific algorithms such as Argon2, bcrypt or scrypt with unique salts resist cracking.
d
Hashing versus encryption
Why is reversible encryption a poor way to store passwords?
Anyone who obtains the key can recover every password
Encryption makes passwords longer than the database allows
Encrypted passwords cannot be checked at login
Encryption is too slow for any login system
Hashing is one-way; encryption is reversible, so key theft exposes all passwords, as the Adobe breach showed.
d
Salts
What does a unique salt per password defeat?
Precomputed rainbow tables and spotting identical passwords
Phishing pages that capture typed passwords
Keyloggers installed on user devices
Brute-force guessing of one user's password
Salts make each hash unique, so precomputed tables and duplicate detection fail. Slow hashing limits guessing.
d
Slow hashing
Why are fast hashes like SHA-256 unsuitable on their own for password storage?
Attackers can test billions of guesses per second
They produce hashes that are too short
They cannot handle passwords with symbols
They are not supported by modern databases
Password hashing should be deliberately slow and memory-hard to raise the cost of cracking.
m
Breach lessons
What made the 2012 LinkedIn password breach so damaging?
Passwords were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes
Passwords were protected by bcrypt with salts
The passwords were never stored anywhere
Users all had multi-factor authentication
Unsalted fast hashes allowed mass cracking.
m
Authentication factors
Which pair represents two different authentication factor types?
A password and a hardware security key
A password and a PIN
A fingerprint and a face scan
Two different passwords
Something you know plus something you have counts as two factors; two knowledge items do not.
d
SMS MFA
Why is SMS-based MFA considered weaker than an authenticator app or security key?
SIM swapping and interception can redirect codes
SMS codes are always longer than six digits
SMS cannot be used on smartphones
SMS codes never expire after use
SMS is better than nothing but is vulnerable to SIM swaps and telecom weaknesses.
d
Phishing-resistant MFA
Why are FIDO2/WebAuthn keys resistant to phishing?
The key signs a challenge bound to the genuine site's origin
The key displays the website's name on a small screen
The key changes the user's password after every login
The key blocks all emails that contain links
Origin binding means a fake site cannot obtain a valid response for the real site.
m
TOTP
What does a TOTP authenticator code depend on?
A shared secret and the current time
The user's password and IP address
The phone's battery level and location
A code sent by SMS from the server
TOTP derives short-lived codes from a shared secret and time steps, typically 30 seconds.
d
MFA fatigue
In the 2022 Uber breach, an attacker repeatedly sent push requests until one was approved. Which control reduces this risk?
Number matching or phishing-resistant MFA
Longer passwords for all employees
Sending more push notifications per hour
Disabling MFA for contractors only
Push fatigue exploits simple approve prompts. Number matching and FIDO2 reduce it.
m
Password managers
What is the main security benefit of a password manager?
It makes unique, strong passwords practical for every site
It removes the need for multi-factor authentication
It prevents phishing emails reaching the inbox
It stores passwords in plain text for easy recovery
Unique passwords stop one breach from compromising other accounts.
m
DAC
In discretionary access control, who decides who can access a resource?
The resource's owner
A central security label
The user's job role only
The attributes of the request
DAC lets owners grant access, as with typical file sharing.
m
MAC
Which access control model enforces system-wide labels such as Secret and Top Secret?
Mandatory access control
Discretionary access control
Role-based access control
Rule-free access control
MAC enforces central classification labels that users cannot override.
d
RBAC
What is a known drawback of role-based access control in large organisations?
Role explosion, with thousands of narrowly defined roles
It cannot assign permissions to groups of users
It requires every user to own their own files
It cannot be audited by any tool
Attempting to model every combination creates too many roles; ABAC adds flexibility.
d
ABAC
Which access rule is an example of attribute-based access control?
Allow if department is Finance, device is managed and time is within working hours
Allow if the file owner has shared the file with the user
Allow if the user is a member of the Administrators role
Allow if the document's label is lower than the user's clearance
ABAC evaluates attributes of the user, resource, action and environment.
m
SSO
What is single sign-on (SSO)?
One authentication that gives access to many applications
One password shared by all employees
One application that holds every company file
One server that stores all backups
SSO uses an identity provider so users authenticate once.
d
Federation
In SAML or OIDC federation, what does the identity provider do?
Authenticates the user and issues an assertion or token to the application
Stores the application's data and serves it to the user
Encrypts the network connection between user and application
Replaces the application's own authorisation logic entirely
The IdP vouches for identity; the service provider trusts its signed assertion and still decides permissions.
d
IDOR
A user changes /invoice?id=1001 to id=1002 and sees another customer's invoice. What is this flaw?
An insecure direct object reference (broken access control)
A cross-site scripting vulnerability
A weak password policy
A denial-of-service flaw
The server failed to check that the user is authorised for the requested object.
m
Privileged accounts
Why are privileged accounts a prime target for attackers?
They grant broad control over systems and data
They are always protected by the weakest passwords
They cannot be monitored by any security tool
They are deleted automatically after each use
Compromising an admin account gives wide access, so PAM controls focus on them.
d
Tiered administration
In Microsoft's tiered administration model, why should a domain admin never log on to a normal workstation?
Credentials left on a lower-tier machine could be stolen and used against Tier 0
Domain admins are not licensed to use workstations
Workstations cannot run administrative tools
Logging on would delete the workstation's profile
Tier separation keeps high-value credentials off machines exposed to everyday threats.
m
Credential vaulting
What does a PAM credential vault do?
Stores privileged passwords and rotates them automatically
Stores users' personal photos and documents
Blocks all administrative access permanently
Shares admin passwords by email when needed
Vaulting with rotation means admins check out credentials that change after use.
d
Session recording
Why do PAM systems record privileged sessions?
To create an accountable record of administrative actions
To make privileged sessions run faster
To replace the need for any authentication
To allow users to replay sessions as entertainment
Recordings support investigation, deterrence and audit of high-risk activity.
d
Account lifecycle
Why should leavers' accounts be disabled automatically through HR-driven provisioning such as SCIM?
Orphaned accounts can be misused long after someone leaves
Disabled accounts improve email delivery speed
Automatic provisioning removes the need for passwords
Leavers' accounts become administrators by default
Timely deprovisioning closes a common access path for former staff and attackers.
m
Access reviews
What is the purpose of periodic access reviews?
Confirming each user still needs the access they hold
Resetting every user's password each quarter
Granting extra rights to long-serving staff
Counting how many logins happen per day
Reviews remove unneeded access and counter privilege creep.
m
Service accounts
Which practice suits a service account used by an application?
Minimal permissions and a managed, rotated credential
Domain admin rights so it never fails
A password that never changes or expires
Interactive logon rights for every developer
Service accounts are frequent targets; least privilege and rotation reduce risk.
d
Zero Trust identity
Why does Zero Trust treat identity as the main control plane?
Access decisions follow the verified user and device, not the network location
Identity systems are the only systems that keep logs
Network firewalls cannot be configured in a Zero Trust design
Identities never change once they have been created
With users and apps everywhere, verified identity and device context replace network trust.
d
Password policy
Which modern password guidance reflects NIST SP 800-63B?
Check new passwords against breached lists and avoid forced periodic changes
Force a change every 30 days with complex composition rules
Limit passwords to a maximum of eight characters
Store password hints alongside the hash
Current guidance favours length, breach screening and change only on evidence of compromise.
